16.7.8 Addition Reactions of Alkynes

16.7.8.1 Hydrogenation

The conditions for hydrogenation of alkynes are similar to those employed for alkenes. In the presence of finely divided platinum, palladium or nickel, two molecules of hydrogen add to the triple bond of an alkyne to yield an alkane. Addition of two molecules of hydrogen to alkynes occurs in two steps, initially forming the corresponding alkenes and finally alkanes.

With efficient catalysts such as platinum, palladium, or nickel, it is usually impossible to stop the reaction at the alkene stage. However, hydrogenation of an alkyne can be stopped at the alkene stage by using a “poisoned” (partially deactivated) catalyst made by treating a good catalyst with a compound that makes the catalyst less effective. Lindlar’s catalyst is a poisoned palladium catalyst; composed of powdered barium sulfate coated with palladium, poisoned with quinoline. In an internal alkyne, syn addition gives a cis-alkene product (if cis/trans-isomerism is possible in product alkene).

Terminal alkynes and acetylene, react with metals such as sodium in liquid ammonia to form salts called alkynides or acetylides (Section 16.7.7). However, reduction of non-terminal alkynes to trans-alkene (anti addition), can be carried by reduction of alkynes with sodium metal in liquid ammonia.

Because of acidic nature, acetylene and 1-alkynes react with ammonical solutions of cuprous chloride and silver nitrate to form acetylides and alkynides of these metals.

Copper and silver acetylides are highly explosive in dry condition. They can, however, be decomposed by acids such as nitric acid to regenerate acetylene. Since non–terminal alkynes do not form alkynides, this reaction can be used as a test to distinguish terminal alkynes from non-terminal alkynes.

16.7.8 Addition Reactions of Alkynes

16.7.8.1 Hydrogenation

The conditions for hydrogenation of alkynes are similar to those employed for alkenes. In the presence of finely divided platinum, palladium or nickel, two molecules of hydrogen add to the triple bond of an alkyne to yield an alkane. Addition of two molecules of hydrogen to alkynes occurs in two steps, initially forming the corresponding alkenes and finally alkanes.

With efficient catalysts such as platinum, palladium, or nickel, it is usually impossible to stop the reaction at the alkene stage. However, hydrogenation of an alkyne can be stopped at the alkene stage by using a “poisoned” (partially deactivated) catalyst made by treating a good catalyst with a compound that makes the catalyst less effective. Lindlar’s catalyst is a poisoned palladium catalyst; composed of powdered barium sulfate coated with palladium, poisoned with quinoline. In an internal alkyne, syn addition gives a cis-alkene product (if cis/trans-isomerism is possible in product alkene).

Tidbit

Syn addition is the addition of two substituents to the same side of a double or triple bond.

16.7.8.2 Reduction by Dissolving Metal

Terminal alkynes and acetylene, react with metals such as sodium in liquid ammonia to form salts called alkynides or acetylides (Section 16.7.7). However, reduction of non-terminal alkynes to trans-alkene (anti addition), can be carried by reduction of alkynes with sodium metal in liquid ammonia.

16.7.8.3 Hydrohalogenation

Two molecules of halogen acids are added to alkynes in two steps, to form geminal dihalides. In case of symmetric alkyne, the second step follows the Markovnikov’s rule. However, addition of halogen acids to asymmetric alkynes follows Markovnikov’s rule in both the steps.
